cards: **W14 · Agentic experiment loops: the reproduction agent's own wall clock.** R1 · physical · top pick · distance SAME · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · REJECT **Question.** Do eight independent attempts by an open-weight agent reproduce many more no-code ML papers than one attempt, or do the same papers keep failing? **What is known.** An ML-engineering benchmark found agents kept improving up to 128 independent 30-minute attempts per task, yet stayed far below top humans; tasks were optimization, not paper reproduction [rebench]. Whether reproduction success rises with repeated attempts on no-code papers is unreported: one benchmark averaged 3 runs [paperbench], another ran each paper once [reclaim_once]. **Hypothesis.** Extra attempts add little because failures are paper-specific: nine of fifteen no-code papers beat all four published benchmark agents [reclaim_index]. **If compute is the lever.** Eight attempts reproduce at least four more of 16 papers than one attempt, and the count still rises between four and eight. **If not.** Eight attempts add at most three of 16 papers over one attempt; roughly ten papers fail every attempt, flat after four attempts. **Test.** Run an open 27B agent up to eight times on each of 16 small no-code reproduction papers on single GH200 GPUs; compare papers reproduced by any attempt with the published single run (2 of 16) and four different agents combined (6 of 15). *Compute axis.* Independent attempts per paper (best-of-k), each on its own GPU: 1–8 attempts, 4 levels. **W6 · Hyperparameter-tuning budget and baseline fairness.** R1 · physical · random pick · distance ADJACENT · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · halted: cost record broken **Question.** Under equal tuning budgets, how many trials per method until a claimed optimizer gain's verdict stops changing, and does parallel early-stopping search reach it faster? **What is known.** Lucic et al. bootstrapped best-of-k over 100 random trials per GAN, finding rankings shift with budget [lucic_budget]; ASHA searched over 1,000 configurations on 25 workers in about 40 minutes [asha_pdf]. No source found measures at which equal trial count a published optimizer claim's verdict stops changing, or whether early-stopping parallel search reaches that verdict sooner than sequential search. **Hypothesis.** A 16-trial equal search per method gives the 1,024-trial verdict, because extra tuning shrank gaps without reversing them in a CPU pilot. **Restructuring.** Model-based search: each of up to 1,024 trials per method waits for earlier trials' results before choosing settings. Asynchronous successive halving starts many settings at once on 8 GPUs and stops weak ones early, so trials need not wait [asha_abs]. **If compute is the lever.** A claimed gain's verdict changes only past 64 trials per method; parallel early-stopping search gets there 3x faster than sequential searches. **If not.** Every verdict at 1,024 trials per method already appears by 16; early-stopping search is under 1.5x faster, pruning slow-starting good settings and picking worse ones. **Test.** Rerun AdamW-versus-SGD and Muon-versus-SGD claims on fast CIFAR-10 training with equal random-search budgets of 1 to 1,024 trials per method, plus same-method and wider-network controls; time parallel early-stopping search against one sequential model-based search and eight side-by-side copies. *Compute axis.* Trials per method in an equal-budget hyperparameter search, i.e. the number of full training runs one verdict needs (also the length of the sequential search chain): 1–1,024 trials per method, 6 levels. Closest prior: 1,000 [asha_pdf]. **Check first.** Parallel early-stopping search's chosen settings give the same accuracy gap as one sequential search, within 0.15 points; stock script first reproduces 94.01% [airbench94_acc] Tolerance: Stock script: 25-run mean within +/-0.06 points of 94.01 (about 2 standard errors at 0.14-point spread). Parallel vs sequential: re-evaluated gap within +/-0.15 points and identical verdict class.. **Would not show.** Only fast CIFAR-10 optimizer claims; LLM-scale or hour-long training runs untested. **I2 · Correctness and confidence probes as a cheap verifier for sampled error flags (plus probe-based early exit).** R1 · interp · top pick · distance SAME · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · halted: cost record broken **Question.** Does a hidden-state correctness probe let more sampled error checks per paper yield higher precision on real, retraction-grade paper errors? **What is known.** SPOT ran 8 independent checks per paper with no verifier: best precision 6.1%; open Qwen3-235B found 38.2% of text-only errors within 4 runs [spot_abs]. Whether a learned verifier, here an activation probe, turns more than 8 samples per paper into higher precision on real errors instead of more false flags. **Hypothesis.** More sampled checks lift precision above 6.1% if a probe on the model's activations, which encode its own correctness, ranks flags. **If compute is the lever.** Probe-chosen top flag per paper is right ≥10 points more often at 64 than 8 samples, and beats frequency voting. **If not.** Probe-chosen top-flag precision stops rising by 8 samples (under 5-point gain to 64) and ties frequency voting, because held-out probe AUROC stays below 0.65. **Test.** Qwen3-32B checks 42 real-error papers 64 times each; a probe trained on planted ML-paper errors ranks pooled flags. Compare top-flag precision at 1-64 samples against frequency voting, log-probability and random choice; anchor by reproducing Qwen3-235B's published recall. *Compute axis.* Independent sampled error checks per paper, pooled before the rankers pick flags: 1–64 samples per paper, 7 levels. Closest prior: 8 [spot_runs]. *Restructuring.* none. **Check first.** Our pipeline reruns open Qwen3-235B on released text-only SPOT papers, 8 runs; recall should match published 15.4% within 6.2 points [spot_qwen]. Follower policies learn concurrently on separate environment blocks; importance weighting lets the leader learn from their data, shortening its chain [sapg_subsample]. **If compute is the lever.** 49,152 environments reach the 24,576 arm's 15,000-update success by 11,250 updates, 4+ successes higher; single-GPU and best-of-six training never reach it. **If not.** 49,152 environments gain under 4 successes at 15,000 updates or need over 13,500 updates to match 24,576, from near-duplicate data or unstable leader updates. **Test.** Train a simulated Allegro hand on a Kuka arm to regrasp objects for 15,000 updates, 4 seeds per arm, with the split-and-aggregate method at 24,576 and 49,152 environments, against plain 8,192-environment training and the best of six independent copies. *Compute axis.* Policy-update cycles (chain length) one training run needs to reach the target success; arms differ in GPUs and environments per update: 2,500–15,000 update cycles, 6 levels. **SEAS-3D · Converged 3D earthquake-cycle (SEAS) simulation.** R3 · physical · top pick · distance SAME · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · REJECT **Question.** In 3D earthquake-cycle simulations, does refining the grid past 4 cells per friction process zone make later earthquake times converge, or do runs keep diverging? **What is known.** The 3D community benchmark compared ten codes at up to 4 cells per process zone and found later recurrence intervals resolution-sensitive [s_jiang]; a 2D study found well-resolved sequences differ [s_lambert]. I found no 3D study refining a complex fault past 4 cells per process zone while measuring perturbation growth; whether divergence is numerical or chaotic is untested. **Hypothesis.** On physically complex faults, tiny differences grow each cycle, so finer grids extend timing agreement by only about one event per halving. **If compute is the lever.** Complex-fault runs at 16 and 32 cells per process zone match every event time within 1%; perturbed copies never diverge. **If not.** Agreement between 16 and 32 cells stalls within 2 events of where 1e-8-perturbed copies diverge, below the run's total, gaining about one event per halving. **Test.** Run a GPU 3D fault-cycle code at 2-32 cells per process zone on a periodic benchmark fault and two complex faults, with perturbed copies. Baseline: published 500-m benchmark runs [s_zenodo]; count how many leading earthquakes stay in step; about 470 USD. *Compute axis.* Grid cells per quasi-static process zone (process-zone length divided by cell size); more cells per step is what more GPU memory bandwidth buys: 2–64 cells per process zone, 6 levels. frontier:
**R1**
- Km-scale climate simulation: resolution and simulated years per day (ELSEWHERE): Resolution (and simulated years): the largest reported is global 3 km for 10 years (https://e3sm.org/eamxx-decadal-run/); whether km-scale resolution actually narrows projection uncertainty is still a hope, not a measurement (https://research-collection.ethz.ch/handle/20.500.11850/389770?show=full).

**R2**
- Model size and pretraining compute for robot foundation models (SAME): More compute buys model size and pretraining compute; the largest reported is 10B+ parameters (https://generalistai.com/blog/gen-0), and it is unknown whether gains continue above ~10B while the real corpus grows only ~10,000 hours per week with no touch channel.
- Video world models as generators of training trajectories (SAME): More compute buys neural trajectories (and video-model size); the largest reported is 240k trajectories at ~81,000 L40 GPU-hours (https://arxiv.org/html/2505.12705v2), and it is unknown whether the log-linear trend continues above that or holds for contact-rich/deformable tasks (https://arxiv.org/html/2512.10675v2).

**R3**
- Archive-scale catalogs and foreshock specificity (SAME): More compute buys catalog depth and coverage; the largest reported is 1.3 PB across 47,354 stations picked (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18874), and it is unknown whether global deep catalogs change the false-alarm rate of foreshock-like activity before M7+ events.

**R5**
- Rigid in-hand dexterity and insertion under domain-randomization curricula (SAME): Simulated experience and parallel environments behind wider randomization: the largest reported are about 13,000 simulated years over several months on 64 V100s plus 920 machines (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1910.07113) and 2x10^10 samples at 24,576 environments (https://arxiv.org/html/2407.20230); it is unknown whether more closes contact-sensitive residuals such as insertion's 64% real versus 99.6% sim.
- Generalist policy (VLA) scaling and its real-world evaluation (SAME): Model size and training compute: the largest reported is 55B parameters, where 5B to 55B raised the unseen-scenario average from 44 to 63 (https://arxiv.org/html/2307.15818); it is unknown whether gains continue above 55B or whether size can replace environment and object diversity (https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.18647).

models (SAME): More compute buys model size and pretraining compute; the largest reported is 10B+ parameters (https://generalistai.com/blog/gen-0), and it is unknown whether gains continue above ~10B
